summaries.gardner: Netflix is a classic past Rule Breaker: the top dog that created streaming, with a strong brand, excellent historical management and a lasting edge. Today it is a mature leader in a no-longer-emerging industry, and the shares are down about 42% over the past year, so it lacks the price momentum and 'emerging industry' traits Gardner prizes, though critics calling it overvalued has long been part of its story.
summaries.buffett: Netflix has a strong consumer brand, pricing power (US price rises in January 2025 and March 2026) and high returns on capital (about 32% ROIC), and it is simple to understand as a subscription business. Against that, it has no long record of steady free cash flow (only since 2020), carries $14.3B of debt against $9.1B of cash, faces fast-changing competition, and at about 22x trailing earnings offers little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would like the scale economics: Netflix spreads about $17B a year of content spend over the largest paying audience and earns a 29.5% operating margin, a self-reinforcing advantage. He would worry about inverting the risks: entertainment tastes change, YouTube and the new Skydance (Paramount plus Warner Bros.) compete hard, and there are no switching costs, so it is a good business at a fair rather than bargain price.
summaries.lynch: Netflix now looks like a stalwart-to-fast-grower hybrid: revenue growth of about 13% in 2026 with earnings growing faster thanks to margin expansion and buybacks. With a forward P/E of about 20 and a PEG near 1.0, Lynch might find the price reasonable, but it is anything but overlooked (52 analysts cover it) and insiders such as co-CEO Ted Sarandos have been selling.
summaries.fisher: Netflix fits much of Fisher's growth checklist: a long sales runway from ads, live events and games, a management team that keeps launching new products (ad tier in 2022, paid sharing, live sports, video podcasts in 2026), strong technology and a famous culture. Weaker points are reduced disclosure (no more member counts) and a less certain multi-year growth path as the core subscription market matures.
summaries.graham: Netflix fails most of Graham's defensive-investor tests: it pays no dividend, trades at about 22x trailing earnings and roughly 9.8x book value (P/E x P/B well above 22.5), and debt exceeds cash. It does pass on size, ten years of continuous profits and long-term EPS growth, but the price offers no Graham-style margin of safety.
summaries.thiel: Netflix once answered Thiel's questions well: it started with a big share of a small market (DVD-by-mail), timed the shift to streaming perfectly and built a durable scale-driven monopoly-like position in paid streaming. Today its technology is not ten times better than rivals' and it competes in a crowded market with YouTube, Amazon, Disney and Skydance, so it looks more like a strong incumbent than a 'zero to one' monopoly.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on durable growth at a fair price with management that is 'fit' on costs; Netflix delivers rising margins (29.5% operating margin in 2025, 31.5% guided for 2026), heavy buybacks and about 13% growth. The roughly 42% share-price fall over the last year has brought valuation down to about 20x forward earnings, though slowing growth and less disclosure have hurt sentiment.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and positive price momentum; Netflix shows neither clearly right now, with revenue growth guided to slow to 11.7% in Q3 2026 and the stock down about 42% over a year. Possible catalysts include the doubling of ad revenue to about $3B in 2026 and margin gains, but the trend and liquidity backdrop do not make it an obvious concentrated bet.
summaries.smith: Netflix meets Terry Smith's 'good company' test in many ways: high returns on capital (about 32% ROIC), strong gross-margin expansion to 48.5%, low capital intensity apart from content and growth from a global brand. The questions are whether content spending is really a recurring cost that limits cash conversion and whether today's roughly 3.8% FCF yield is 'not overpaying' for 12-14% growth.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Netflix has a high return on capital (about 32% ROIC) but only a modest earnings yield, with EV/EBIT around 21x (about 4.8%). That combination ranks it as a good business at a fair price rather than the cheap, high-return stock the formula seeks.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool fits fairly well: a good business with high returns, talented long-tenured managers (Sarandos since 2000, Peters since 2008) and strong reinvestment options in ads, live and games plus buybacks ($4.7B in Q2 2026). The weakest leg is that much reinvestment goes into content whose returns are hard to measure, and the co-CEO structure adds some uncertainty.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks simple businesses in temporary distress bought at deep discounts with little downside; Netflix is simple and its shares have fallen sharply, but at about 22x trailing earnings it is not a deep-value 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' bet. The setback (slowing growth after the password-sharing boost, losing Warner Bros. to Paramount) looks partly temporary but not mispriced enough for his style.
summaries.wood: Netflix is not a core ARK-style disruptive-innovation play today: it is a mature streaming leader rather than a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomic sequencing. It does use AI in recommendations and production (it bought AI filmmaking firm InterPositive in 2026), but its market is unlikely to grow many times larger in five years.
summaries.ackman: Netflix fits much of Ackman's checklist: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating business with a dominant market position, pricing power and high barriers to entry, and Pershing Square itself owned the stock in 2022. The negatives are debt above cash, a valuation that is fair rather than deeply discounted, and competitive pressure from YouTube and the merged Skydance.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for scale economies shared with customers; Netflix spreads its content budget over the biggest audience and offers a cheap ad tier ($8.99 in the US), but it has raised prices repeatedly rather than passing scale savings back to customers like Costco or Amazon. Its long-term position looks durable but not clearly stronger in 10-20 years than today given new well-funded rivals.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine backed huge markets and products that solve a real problem; Netflix's market (global TV and entertainment time) is huge, but entertainment is a want rather than a painful problem, and the company is long past the start-up stage. It would mainly appeal as an example of a company that rode a big platform shift (broadband streaming) at the right time.
summaries.nash: On Tom Nash's process Netflix scores well on quality (29.5% operating margin, 13-16% revenue growth, strong moat and culture) but trips several hard rules: debt ($14.3B) exceeds cash ($9.1B), it has a co-CEO structure, and his DCF at a 12% discount rate gives roughly $38 a share versus a $70.57 price. Its 5-year return also trails the S&P 500 after a roughly 42% fall over the past year.

momentum.evidence: NFLX closed at $70.57 on Oct 14, 2026, down about 42% over 52 weeks (range $65.08-$124.86), far behind the market.

g4.evidence: Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters have long, successful tenures and the company is ~83% institutionally owned, but founder Reed Hastings left the board in June 2026 and no famous activist or partner currently anchors the stock.

g6.evidence: Netflix has long been called overvalued, but after the 2026 sell-off most of its 52 covering analysts rate it a Buy with an average $92 target, and Huber Research downgraded it to Sell on Oct 13, 2026.

simple.evidence: It sells monthly streaming subscriptions (plus ads) to households, and spends on content and technology, which a generalist can easily understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue has grown every year (e.g. $25.0B in 2020 to $45.2B in 2025) and it has been profitable for well over a decade, but free cash flow was negative until 2020 and growth stalled in 2022.

integrity.evidence: Netflix's long-form shareholder letters are known for candour and it walked away from Warner Bros. rather than overpay (collecting a $2.8B fee), but it cut disclosure by dropping member counts in 2025 and moving engagement reports to annual from 2027.

b6.evidence: Netflix historically built rather than bought, but its 2025-26 bid for Warner Bros.' studios and HBO (backed by a $42.2B bridge loan) was a large empire-style move it ultimately abandoned when Paramount outbid it.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 32% and ROE about 50% on the latest twelve months, with interest coverage of about 17x, so returns do not depend on leverage.

fcf.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was $9.46B ($10.15B operating cash flow less $0.69B capex) against $10.98B of net income, about 86% conversion, though heavy content spend historically held conversion lower.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings rose to $42.3B by end-2025 while annual net income grew from $2.76B (2020) to $10.98B (2025), and market value (~$294B) is far above cumulative retained earnings.

safety.evidence: A conservative DCF (12.7% growth, 19.7% FCF margin, 12% discount) gives about $38 a share versus the $70.57 price, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: At about 20x forward earnings, 21x EV/EBIT and a 3.8% FCF yield for 13% revenue growth and expanding margins, the price looks reasonable rather than cheap.

mu5.evidence: Failure paths include losing viewing time to YouTube and short video, a content-cost war with Skydance, Disney and Amazon, and price-rise fatigue, but its scale and profits make outright failure unlikely.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in ads, live events, games and international content, but much of its cash now goes to buybacks ($9.1B in 2025, $4.7B in Q2 2026) because high-return reinvestment needs are limited.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart-like fast grower: a global streaming leader growing revenue about 13% with expanding margins, a simple story of more price, more ads and more members.

ly3.evidence: The forward P/E of about 20 is close to expected EPS growth, giving a PEG of about 0.96.

runway.evidence: Advertising is expected to roughly double to about $3B in 2026 and Netflix is pushing into live sports, games and video podcasts, with consensus revenue rising to about $63B by 2028.

ly7.evidence: Diluted share count fell about 1.5% year on year through buybacks, but insiders are net sellers, including co-CEO Ted Sarandos selling over 100,000 shares in August 2026.

ly8.evidence: Netflix is one of the most widely followed stocks, covered by about 52 analysts and about 83% owned by institutions.

fi2.evidence: It launched the ad tier (2022), paid sharing (2023), live events such as NFL Christmas games and WWE Raw, TV games and Netflix Playground (2026) and video podcasts (2026).

fi3.evidence: Technology and development spend of $3.39B in 2025 underpins its recommendation engine, ad-tech stack (built in-house in 2025) and Open Connect delivery network, which support a 29.5% operating margin.

fi4.evidence: Its marketing and cultural reach make hits such as Squid Game and KPop Demon Hunters global events, but its ad sales operation is still young, with about 4,000 ad clients in early 2026.

longterm.evidence: Netflix has repeatedly invested ahead of profits (original content from 2013, local productions in 50+ countries, live sports and games) and its culture emphasises long-term value.

gr1.evidence: Netflix had $45.2B of revenue in 2025 and a market value of about $294B in October 2026.

ni10.evidence: Netflix reported a net profit in every year from 2016 to 2025, rising to $10.98B in 2025.

gr4.evidence: Netflix has never paid a cash dividend, as its 2025 10-K confirms.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS reached $2.53 in 2025 (split-adjusted) versus well under $0.10 split-adjusted a decade earlier, far more than a one-third increase.

gr6.evidence: The shares trade at about 22x trailing EPS of $3.17 and about 28x 2025 EPS of $2.53, above Graham's 15x limit.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 22 times P/B of about 9.75 gives roughly 217, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Netflix's streaming technology and recommendations are excellent, but not ten times better than YouTube, Amazon or Disney's platforms.

timing.evidence: Streaming reached 48.5% of US TV viewing in June 2026 and connected-TV advertising is growing, but the core subscription market is maturing and growth is slowing to about 12-14%.

th3.evidence: Netflix dominated the small DVD-by-mail and early streaming market, then expanded to over 190 countries and into originals, ads, live and games.

team.evidence: Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters are highly regarded and have expanded margins from 20.6% (2023) to 29.5% (2025), but they are successors rather than the founder.

th5.evidence: It sells directly to consumers through its own app built into almost every smart TV (often with a Netflix button on the remote) and through bundles with telecom partners such as Mercado Libre in 2026.

durable.evidence: Its brand, scale and library should keep it a top-three global entertainment platform, but YouTube's creator video, AI-generated content and short-form video could erode its share of viewing over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Streaming's potential is now obvious to every media and tech giant, so Netflix's original unique insight no longer gives it a secret opportunity.

trend.evidence: Netflix is a leading beneficiary of the shift from linear TV to streaming, but it is not a leading AI or cloud beneficiary.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth is guided to slow from 16% in 2025 to 13-14% in 2026 and 11.7% in Q3 2026, and Morgan Stanley cut its target from $83 to $80 in October 2026.

dr2.evidence: Margins (31.5% guided for 2026) and ad revenue (~$3B) should keep improving, but slowing subscription growth and the new Skydance rival are well known.

dr4.evidence: Streaming is a low-cost form of entertainment that held up in past slowdowns, but the stock's 1.6 beta and ad exposure make it sensitive to the economy and rates.

dr6.evidence: Q3 2026 results on Oct 20, 2026, the ad-revenue ramp, big live events (e.g. Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua) and continued $27.1B buyback authorization could all drive results.

dr7.evidence: With falling price momentum, decelerating growth and a crowded competitive field, conviction is not high enough for a concentrated Druckenmiller-style bet.

gm.evidence: Gross margin rose from 38.9% in 2020 to 48.5% in 2025, a sign of pricing power and scale, though it is lower than software-like businesses because content costs sit in cost of revenues.

fcfyield.evidence: The FCF yield is about 3.8% on trailing free cash flow of $11.15B (boosted by the $2.8B Warner Bros. fee), reasonable for a business growing revenue about 13%.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $14.35B against an enterprise value of about $301B gives an EV/EBIT of about 21x (a ~4.8% earnings yield).

pa2.evidence: The 2026 sell-off reflects slowing growth after the password-sharing boost and losing Warner Bros. to Paramount, which may prove temporary, though competitive pressure from YouTube is structural.

pa4.evidence: With $45.2B of revenue, a 29.5% operating margin, about 17x interest coverage and a dominant brand, the chance of permanent capital loss from business failure is small, though valuation losses are possible.

wo1.evidence: Netflix is an entertainment streamer, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing, despite using AI tools (e.g. the 2026 InterPositive acquisition).

wo2.evidence: Its unit costs per member fall with scale, but it has been raising prices rather than cutting them to unlock big new demand.

wo3.evidence: It mainly operates one platform (streaming video) with adjacent ads, games and live events rather than several converging innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Consensus expects revenue of about $63B by 2028 versus $45.2B in 2025, solid growth but not a market many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: As a subscription and content business it uses no commodities and has mostly fixed-rate senior notes, though foreign-exchange swings affect reported revenue.

ns1.evidence: Netflix shares scale through a low-price ad plan ($8.99 in the US) and more content per dollar, but it has raised prices repeatedly (latest US increase in March 2026) rather than passing savings back.

ns4.evidence: Its scale and ad business should strengthen it, but the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. into Skydance and YouTube's growth mean its relative position may not be clearly stronger in 10-20 years.

va2.evidence: It solves the everyday problem of finding good, affordable entertainment on demand, which is large but not a painful need.

tn1.evidence: Netflix was built for the streaming shift and leads it, but streaming is not an infrastructure-layer AI, energy or robotics trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees a slowing subscription streamer, while Netflix is becoming an advertising, live-events and games platform, though the gap is modest.

tn3.evidence: It is a ~$294B US large cap, not Chinese, not a commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or start-up.

tn4.evidence: Revenue has grown every year and it is profitable ($10.98B net income in 2025); it fails only on cash versus debt ($9.1B cash vs $14.3B debt in June 2026), a manageable gap given ~$9.5B annual FCF.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive every recent quarter (e.g. $1.53B in Q2 2026), but debt has exceeded cash throughout, e.g. $14.3B vs $9.1B at June 30, 2026.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 17x, the current ratio about 1.19 and liabilities about 1.09x equity at end-2025, but total assets of $55.6B were only about 1.92x total liabilities of $29.0B, just short of 2x.

tn18.evidence: Sarandos and Peters have a strong execution record, but neither is the founder, they have been co-CEOs only since 2020 and 2023, and they have sold rather than bought shares on the open market.

tn20.evidence: Netflix beat EPS estimates in Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 and was in line in Q2 2026 ($0.80 vs ~$0.79), but missed in Q3 2025 because of a Brazilian tax charge and has disappointed on guidance.

tn21.evidence: It has a co-CEO structure (Sarandos and Peters), a red flag in Nash's list, and insiders have been selling while the stock fell, although there is no fraud suspicion, auditor change (Ernst & Young) or margin decline.

tn22.evidence: Netflix has $45B+ of revenue, strong profits and shrinks its share count through buybacks rather than issuing stock.

tn24.evidence: At $70.57, a reverse DCF with a ~19.7% FCF margin and 10% discount rate implies about 21% annual revenue growth, above the 13-16% Netflix is delivering (though rising margins narrow the gap).

tn25.evidence: Using a 3-year average growth of 12.7%, FCF margin of 19.7%, 4% terminal growth, a 12% discount rate and net debt of $5.2B, the value is about $38 a share, below the $70.57 price.

tn26.evidence: The forward P/E of about 20 sits near media and internet peers and the PEG is about 0.96, just under 1, so it is fairly but not compellingly priced.
